facts.one_liner: Shah Jahan’s white-marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal, mirrored in the charbagh pools.
facts.why_go: The hero photo is the Taj Mahal’s ivory marble tomb rising beyond the formal Mughal garden, its dome and four minarets doubled in the long reflecting pool—the classic Agra view from the southern approach. UNESCO records the mausoleum built on the Yamuna’s right bank between 1631 and 1648 by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, set in a nearly 17-hectare charbagh whose walkways and water channels frame that distant, perfectly symmetrical silhouette. The main gateway, mosque, and guest house complete the complex; light shifts the marble from soft dawn pink to midday white. Enter via the Eastern or Western Gate; the southern gate is exit only.
facts.best_time: October–March for cooler weather; arrive at opening (about 30 minutes before sunrise) for soft light on the reflection and thinner crowds. Closed to general visitors on Fridays. Winter fog can mute the view—check local forecasts.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Agra. About 6 km from Agra Cantt railway station and roughly 8–13 km from Agra Airport (Kheria); ISBT is nearby. Petrol/diesel vehicles stop about 500 m short—use battery buses or golf carts from Shilpgram (Eastern Gate) or Western Gate parking. ASI e-tickets available online.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable Archaeological Survey of India monument; timed/ticketed entry (no prices listed here). Optional paid access into the main mausoleum chamber. Free entry for children under 15 per official rules. Night viewing only on full-moon dates and adjacent days (not Fridays or during Ramzan)—confirm on tajmahal.gov.in.

facts.one_liner: Jinshanling’s Ming watchtowers snaking over Hebei ridges—the photographer’s Wall stretch.
facts.why_go: The hero photo shows the Great Wall at Jinshanling: brick battlements and dense watchtowers climbing green mountain ridges in a long, undulating line—not the crowded Badaling or Mutianyu cable-car plazas. Jinshanling sits in Luanping County, Hebei, about 130 km northeast of central Beijing, linking toward Simatai and Gubeikou; Chinese tourism sources call it a Ming-era essence section rebuilt under Qi Jiguang’s command in the late 16th century, with dozens of enemy towers along roughly 10 km of wall. UNESCO inscribed the Great Wall for its Ming masonry mastery and 2,000-year defensive history. Half-restored, half-wild stretches make this the classic hiking-and-photography panorama matching the image.
facts.best_time: Spring and autumn (especially May–June for green hills; October for clearer views and cooler hiking). Summer heat is intense on exposed stone; winter can bring ice and snow on steep steps.
facts.how_to_get_there: Day trip from Beijing: direct Jinshanling tourist coaches from Dongzhimen (and seasonal weekend buses from Wangjing West), private car (~2–2.5 hours via Jingcheng Expressway), or rail to Gubeikou then taxi (~20 minutes). Confirm same-day return schedules before hiking—transport is scarcer than at Mutianyu.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable scenic area; ticketed entry at the gate (no prices listed). Wear sturdy shoes—steps and unrestored sections are steep. Cable car operates seasonally at some gates; sunrise access may require earlier main-gate hours—verify with the scenic area. Part of the UNESCO Great Wall serial property.

facts.one_liner: Neolithic sarsen circle on Salisbury Plain—lintels and uprights in open grassland.
facts.why_go: The hero photo is Stonehenge’s sarsen circle from a wide landscape angle: massive sandstone uprights capped with lintels on the chalk downland, the silhouette English Heritage calls the world’s most famous prehistoric monument. The first henge earthwork dates to about 3000 BC; the unique stone settings—outer sarsen circle and inner horseshoe, with bluestones between—were erected around 2500 BC in the late Neolithic. Together with Avebury it forms a UNESCO World Heritage landscape dense with prehistoric monuments. During normal hours you follow the visitor path (as close as ~5 m); separate Stone Circle Experience tickets allow limited inside access at the start or end of day.
facts.best_time: Weekday early or late timed slots for quieter paths and softer light. The circle is fully exposed—wrap warmly year-round. Summer evenings stay open later; last ticket sales are earlier than closing to allow the shuttle or walk back.
facts.how_to_get_there: Train from London Waterloo to Salisbury (~90 minutes), then Stonehenge Tour bus or taxi; driving via A303 (visitor centre postcode SP4 7DE). Shuttle buses run every few minutes from the Visitor Centre to the stones (~5–10 minutes), or walk ~2.6 miles (4 km) round trip through National Trust landscape.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable English Heritage site; advance timed tickets strongly recommended (no prices listed). National Trust (England) members enter free with booking rules. Stick to the path to protect buried archaeology and lichens. No toilets at the stones—use the Visitor Centre.

facts.one_liner: Almohad Koutoubia minaret—Marrakech’s landmark tower with green tile band and three orbs.
facts.why_go: The hero centers on the Koutoubia Mosque’s square red-stone minaret: scalloped arches, a turquoise-green zellij band near the top, lantern, and the distinctive finial of three metal spheres. Extending beside it are the mosque’s brick walls and, in the foreground, excavated pillar bases from the earlier Almohad mosque phase. Non-Muslims cannot enter the prayer hall or climb the minaret, but the gardens, esplanade, and exterior views are the classic Marrakech landmark walk west of Jemaa el-Fnaa. The mosque is a defining monument of the Medina of Marrakesh UNESCO site.
facts.best_time: Late afternoon light warms the pink stone; mornings are quieter around the gardens. Summer days are very hot—plan exterior walks early or near sunset. Ramadan and prayer times affect street energy but exterior viewing remains possible.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Marrakech. The minaret is a short walk west of Jemaa el-Fnaa / the medina; taxis and petits taxis drop nearby. Pair with a medina and square evening visit.
facts.good_to_know: Respect that it is an active mosque—photograph exteriors courteously; do not attempt non-Muslim entry. Gardens and ruin field are open-air; stay outside railings. Call to prayer from the minaret is part of the city’s soundscape.

facts.one_liner: Buda Castle palace and green dome on Castle Hill—Budapest view from Gellért Hill.
facts.why_go: The hero is an elevated view of Buda Castle (Budavári Palota) from Gellért Hill: the long palace complex with its pale façades and distinctive teal-green dome and roofs, set on fortified Castle Hill above tree-covered slopes, with the Castle Quarter and Matthias Church spire behind. This is the royal palace quarter of Buda—not a generic Danube skyline crop. UNESCO includes the Buda Castle Quarter in the Budapest World Heritage property. Museums (including the Hungarian National Gallery and Budapest History Museum wings) occupy parts of the palace; the hill itself is free to walk.
facts.best_time: Late spring through early autumn for clear Gellért Hill viewpoints; golden hour lights the palace. Winter can be icy on Castle Hill paths but offers crisp views. Weekday mornings are quieter in museum courtyards.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Budapest. Reach Castle Hill by the Castle Hill Funicular from Clark Ádám tér, bus 16/16A/116, or walking paths from the Chain Bridge area. Gellért Hill viewpoints (for this photo angle) are a separate climb or bus ride on the opposite Buda side.
facts.good_to_know: Palace courtyards and ramparts are largely outdoor; individual museums have separate tickets and hours (see budavar.abtk.hu and museum sites). Wear comfortable shoes for cobbles. Pair with Fisherman’s Bastion / Matthias Church in the same Castle Quarter visit.

facts.one_liner: Pyramid of the Sun on Teotihuacan’s Avenue of the Dead—massive volcanic step pyramid.
facts.why_go: The hero is the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan: a vast multi-tier volcanic-stone step pyramid with a central staircase and fore-platform, photographed from the plaza along the Avenue of the Dead. This is the Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan UNESCO site in the State of Mexico—not the Pyramid of the Moon (smaller, at the avenue’s north end) and not a Maya city. Teotihuacan was one of Mesoamerica’s largest urban centers in the early centuries CE. Climbing access on major pyramids is often restricted—confirm current INAH rules; viewing from the avenue remains the core visit.
facts.best_time: Morning opening beats heat and tour-bus crowds; dry season (roughly November–April) is clearest. Midday sun on the open avenue is intense year-round—hat and water essential.
facts.how_to_get_there: Usual overnight hub is Mexico City (~40–50 km / about an hour by bus from Terminal Norte or by tour/hire car). Day trips are standard; some visitors stay in San Juan Teotihuacán closer to the gates.
facts.good_to_know: Primary subject is Pyramid of the Sun, not the Moon. Buy tickets at official INAH channels; balloon and vendor pitches outside are optional. Altitude and stairs (where open) demand pacing. No prices listed here—they change; check INAH the day you go.

facts.one_liner: Neo-Gothic Las Lajas basilica bridging the Guáitara gorge at Ipiales—not Bogotá.
facts.why_go: The hero shows the Sanctuary of Las Lajas (Santuario de Las Lajas): a grey-and-white neo-Gothic basilica built into the cliff and spanning the Guáitara River gorge on a high arched bridge, with zig-zag paths down the canyon wall. It sits outside Ipiales in Nariño Department near the Ecuador border—not a Bogotá church. The present stone sanctuary dates to the early–mid 20th century on a longstanding Marian pilgrimage site and is on UNESCO’s Tentative List. Free to approach; a local cable car offers an alternate gorge view.
facts.best_time: Dry months are easier for canyon paths; mornings offer clearer light in the gorge. Major feast days and weekends draw pilgrimage crowds. Afternoons can bring mist in the canyon.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Ipiales (or cross-border from Tulcán, Ecuador). The sanctuary is roughly 7 km from Ipiales by taxi, colectivo, or tour; walk/cable car options connect the rim and gorge floor. Nearest major airport hubs are often reached via Pasto or Ecuadorian routes—plan the last leg to Ipiales.
facts.good_to_know: Dress for a pilgrimage church; expect stairs and uneven paths into the gorge. Confirm cable-car hours/fares on laslajas.org if you use it. Distinct from Bogotá’s colonial churches—this is the Ipiales gorge basilica.
